questions.question: In the male reproductive system, where does sperm formation take place?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Testes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **testes** are the primary reproductive organs in the male reproductive system, functioning as the site for both **sperm production** and the secretion of male sex hormones.
 
• Sperm formation, scientifically known as **spermatogenesis**, takes place within specialized structures called **seminiferous tubules** located inside the **testes**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Testes.***
 
• Each testis contains hundreds of **seminiferous tubules** where **male germ cells** (spermatogonia) undergo meiotic division to eventually transform into mature **spermatozoa**.
 
• Apart from sperm production, the **testes** contain **Leydig cells** (interstitial cells) that produce **testosterone**, the hormone responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics and the stimulation of **sperm maturation**.
 
• The **testes** are housed in the **scrotum**, which is situated outside the abdominal cavity to maintain an environment conducive to **sperm viability**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Vas Deferens**:
 
 
• The **vas deferens** is a long, muscular tube that travels from the **epididymis** into the pelvic cavity.
 
• Its primary function is to **transport mature sperm** to the **urethra** in preparation for ejaculation. It does not produce sperm. ***Hence, option 1 is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Seminal Vesicles**:
 
 
• These are a pair of simple tubular glands located posteroinferior to the urinary bladder of males.
 
• They secrete a significant portion of the fluid that ultimately becomes **semen**. This fluid is rich in **fructose**, which provides energy for **sperm motility**. ***Hence, option 3 is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Scrotum**:
 
 
• The **scrotum** is a pouch-like sac of skin that hangs behind the penis and contains the **testes**.
 
• It acts as a **climate control system**, keeping the temperature of the testes slightly lower than the rest of the body, which is essential for **normal sperm development**. ***Hence, option 4 is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Epididymis**:
 
 
• This is a long, coiled tube that rests on the backside of each testis.
 
• It functions in the **storage and maturation** of sperm cells that are produced by the testes. Sperm gain the ability to move (motility) while passing through this duct.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Temperature Regulation**: The **scrotum** maintains the temperature of the **testes** at **2 to 2.5 degrees Celsius** lower than the internal **body temperature** (37 degrees Celsius), which is a prerequisite for successful **spermatogenesis**.
 
• **Sertoli Cells**: Located within the **seminiferous tubules**, these cells are often called "nurse cells" because they provide **nourishment** and structural support to the developing **sperm cells**.
 
• **Hormonal Regulation**: The process of sperm formation is regulated by hormones from the **anterior pituitary gland**, specifically **Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)** and **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)**, which respond to **GnRH** from the **hypothalamus**.
 
• **Puberty**: In males, the production of sperm usually begins at **puberty** (typically between ages **12 and 15**) and continues throughout the individual's life, although the quality and quantity may decline with **age**.
</ul

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes between plant and animal tissues?

options.text: Animal tissues are mostly dead, while plant tissues are mostly living
Both plant and animal tissues have equal growth throughout the body
Plant tissues have no supportive structure, while animals lack living tissues
Plant tissues have dead supportive cells, while animal tissues are mostly living

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Plant tissues have dead supportive cells, while animal tissues are mostly living**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Plants** are **stationary** or sedentary organisms. Since they do not move, they require a large amount of **supportive tissue** for structural strength. Most of these supportive tissues, such as **Sclerenchyma** and **Xylem vessels**, consist of **dead cells**. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.***
 
• **Animals**, on the other hand, move around in search of food, mates, and shelter. This **locomotion** requires a significant amount of **energy**. Consequently, most tissues in animals are **living** to support active **metabolic processes**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• In **plants**, **growth** is restricted to certain regions called **meristems** (Apical, Lateral, and Intercalary). In **animals**, cell growth is more **uniform** throughout the body, and there is no such demarcation of dividing and non-dividing regions. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Plant tissues** possess a highly rigid **supportive structure** due to the presence of **cell walls** made of **cellulose**. Animals lack these dead cell walls and instead rely on living tissues like **connective** and **muscular** tissues for movement and support. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The **structural organization** of organs and organ systems is far more **specialized** and localized in **complex animals** than in plants, reflecting their different feeding methods and active lifestyles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Plant Tissue Classification:**
 
 
• **Meristematic Tissues:** These are **actively dividing** cells found at growing tips. They are **living** and have thin walls with dense cytoplasm.
 
• **Permanent Tissues:** These are derived from meristematic tissues but have lost the ability to divide. They include **Parenchyma** (living), **Collenchyma** (living), and **Sclerenchyma** (dead).
 
• **Complex Tissues:** Include **Xylem** (mostly dead cells like tracheids and vessels) and **Phloem** (mostly living cells like sieve tubes and companion cells).
 
 
 
• **Animal Tissue Classification:**
 
 
• **Epithelial Tissue:** Protective tissues covering the body surface and lining internal organs.
 
• **Connective Tissue:** Tissues like **blood**, **bone**, and **cartilage** that bind and support other tissues.
 
• **Muscular Tissue:** Responsible for movement; includes **striated**, **smooth**, and **cardiac** muscles.
 
• **Nervous Tissue:** Composed of **neurons** that transmit stimuli rapidly from one place to another within the body.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Energy Consumption:** Animals consume much more **ATP** (energy) than plants because of **voluntary movement** and complex internal organ functions like **digestion** and **circulation**.
 
• **Maintenance:** Because many plant cells are **dead**, they require **less maintenance** and can provide **mechanical strength** for long periods (e.g., the **trunk** of a tree).
 
• **Cell Wall vs. Cell Membrane:** The defining feature of **plant tissues** at the microscopic level is the **cellulose cell wall**, which provides **turgidity** and **protection**, a feature entirely absent in **animal tissues**.
 
• **Pattern of Growth:** Animals usually stop growing after reaching **maturity**, whereas many plants continue to grow throughout their **lifespan** due to persistent **meristematic activity**.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is a general property of ionic compounds?

options.text: They are soft and have low melting points
They are insoluble in water and conduct electricity in solid state
They are brittle and conduct electricity in molten or aqueous state
They exist as molecules and have weak interatomic forces

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They are brittle and conduct electricity in molten or aqueous state**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Brittleness**: **Ionic compounds** are generally **hard** but **brittle**. This is because when external **pressure** is applied to an ionic crystal, the layers of ions shift slightly. This shifting brings ions of the **same charge** next to each other, leading to strong **repulsive forces** that cause the crystal to shatter. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• **Electrical Conductivity**: **Ionic compounds** do not conduct **electricity** in the **solid state** because the ions are held firmly in a **fixed position** by strong **electrostatic forces** and cannot move. However, they conduct electricity in the **molten state** or when **dissolved in water (aqueous state)** because the heat or the solvent overcomes the inter-ionic attractions, allowing **ions** to move freely towards the electrodes. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect regarding the solid state.***
 
• **Melting and Boiling Points**: These compounds have very **high melting** and **boiling points**. This is due to the presence of a vast amount of **energy** required to break the strong **inter-ionic attraction** or **electrostatic forces** that hold the **cations** and **anions** together. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Solubility**: **Electrovalent** or **ionic compounds** are generally **soluble in water** (a polar solvent) and **insoluble** in organic solvents like **kerosene**, **petrol**, or **benzene**. 
 
• **Physical State**: Unlike **covalent compounds**, **ionic compounds** do not exist as discrete **molecules**. Instead, they form a **three-dimensional crystal lattice** structure composed of alternating positive and negative ions. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Formation of Ionic Bonds**: An **ionic bond** is formed by the **complete transfer** of one or more **electrons** from a **metal** atom to a **non-metal** atom. The metal loses electrons to become a **positively charged cation**, while the non-metal gains electrons to become a **negatively charged anion**.
 
• **Crystal Lattice**: In the solid state, ionic compounds are arranged in a **regular geometric pattern** called a **crystal lattice**. For example, in **Sodium Chloride (NaCl)**, each **Sodium ion (Na+)** is surrounded by six **Chloride ions (Cl-)** and vice versa.
 
• **Lattice Energy**: This is the **amount of energy** released when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from its constituent **gaseous ions**. A higher **lattice energy** usually corresponds to higher **melting points** and greater stability of the compound.
 
• **Common Examples**:
 
 
• **Sodium Chloride (NaCl)**: Known as common salt, used in food and as a preservative.
 
• **Magnesium Chloride (MgCl2)**: Used in dust control and road stabilization.
 
• **Calcium Oxide (CaO)**: Known as quicklime, widely used in the **steel** and **chemical industries**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Covalent Compounds**: Unlike ionic compounds, **covalent compounds** are formed by the **sharing of electrons**, usually have **lower melting points**, and are often **poor conductors** of electricity in any state because they do not contain **free ions**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The strength of the **ionic bond** depends on the **electronegativity difference** between the two bonding atoms; the greater the difference, the stronger the ionic character.
 
• **Aqueous solutions** of ionic compounds are called **electrolytes** because they facilitate the flow of **electric current** through the migration of **charged particles**.
 
• Ionic compounds are often used as **reagents** in laboratory settings and play crucial roles in **biological systems**, such as **Potassium (K+)** and **Sodium (Na+)** ions which are essential for **nerve impulse transmission**.
</ul

questions.question: Which rule is used to find the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fleming’s left-hand rule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule** is a simple visualization tool used to determine the direction of the **mechanical force** (or motion) exerted on a **current-carrying conductor** when it is placed within an external **magnetic field**.
 
• According to this rule, if we stretch the **thumb**, **forefinger** (index finger), and **middle finger** of the **left hand** such that they are **mutually perpendicular** (at 90 degrees) to each other, their orientations represent specific physical quantities.
 
• The **Forefinger** represents the direction of the **Magnetic Field** (from North pole to South pole).
 
• The **Middle Finger** represents the direction of the **Current** (the flow of positive charge).
 
• The **Thumb** represents the direction of the **Force** or the **Motion** of the conductor. ***Hence, the correct answer is Fleming’s left-hand rule.***
 
• This principle is the fundamental operational basis for the **Electric Motor**, where electrical energy is converted into mechanical work.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fleming’s Right-Hand Rule:**
 
 
• This rule is used to find the direction of **induced current** when a conductor moves inside a magnetic field.
 
• It is primarily applied in **Electric Generators**. In this rule, the **thumb** represents the motion of the conductor, the **forefinger** represents the field, and the **middle finger** represents the **induced current**.
 
 
 
• **Ohm’s Law:**
 
 
• Formulated by **Georg Simon Ohm** in **1827**, it states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, provided physical conditions like **temperature** remain constant (**V = IR**).
 
• It defines the concept of **electrical resistance** and is fundamental to circuit analysis but does not determine the direction of physical force.
 
 
 
• **Lenz’s Law:**
 
 
• Named after **Heinrich Lenz**, who formulated it in **1834**. It states that the direction of an **induced EMF** (Electromotive Force) is such that it always opposes the change in **magnetic flux** that caused it.
 
• It is a manifestation of the **Law of Conservation of Energy**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:** Both the left-hand and right-hand rules were established by **John Ambrose Fleming** in the late **19th century**. He was an English electrical engineer and physicist who also invented the vacuum tube.
 
• **Lorentz Force:** The physical phenomenon behind Fleming's Left-Hand Rule is the **Lorentz Force**. The magnitude of this force (**F**) is given by the formula **F = BIl sinθ**, where **B** is magnetic flux density, **I** is current, **l** is the length of the conductor, and **θ** is the angle between the conductor and the field.
 
• **Maximum Force:** The force experienced by the conductor is **maximum** when the direction of current is **perpendicular** (90 degrees) to the magnetic field.
 
• **Zero Force:** If the current-carrying conductor is placed **parallel** to the magnetic field, the force acting on it is **zero**.

questions.question: In which of the following metals will the rate of formation of bubbles be fastest when it reacts with dil. HCl?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mg**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The rate of formation of bubbles when a metal reacts with **dilute Hydrochloric Acid (HCl)** depends entirely on the **chemical reactivity** of that specific metal.
 
• When metals react with **dilute HCl**, they displace **hydrogen** from the acid, resulting in the evolution of **Hydrogen gas (H2)** in the form of bubbles and the formation of a **metal chloride** salt.
 
• According to the **Reactivity Series** of metals, **Magnesium (Mg)** is positioned higher than **Aluminum (Al)**, **Zinc (Zn)**, and **Iron (Fe)**. This means **Magnesium** is the most chemically active among the given options.
 
• Because **Magnesium** is highly reactive, its reaction with **dilute HCl** is very vigorous and **exothermic**, leading to the **fastest rate** of bubble formation. ***Hence, the statement regarding Mg is correct.***
 
• The chemical equation for this reaction is **Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2**. The rapid evolution of **H2 gas** causes intense effervescence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Reactivity Order:** For the metals provided in the options, the decreasing order of reactivity with **dilute acids** is **Mg > Al > Zn > Fe**.
 
 
• **Magnesium (Mg):** Reacts very rapidly at **room temperature**.
 
• **Aluminum (Al):** It initially reacts slowly due to the presence of a tough, protective layer of **Aluminum Oxide (Al2O3)** on its surface. Once this layer is dissolved by the acid, the reaction becomes vigorous but remains slower than **Magnesium**.
 
• **Zinc (Zn):** Reacts at a moderate rate, slower than both **Magnesium** and **Aluminum**.
 
• **Iron (Fe):** Reacts slowly with **dilute HCl**, producing bubbles at a much lower frequency compared to the others.
 
 
 
• **Hydrogen Gas Test:** The bubbles formed during these reactions consist of **Hydrogen gas**. This can be confirmed by bringing a **burning candle** or splinter near the mouth of the test tube; the gas burns with a distinct **"pop" sound**.
 
• **No Reaction:** Metals that are placed below **Hydrogen** in the reactivity series, such as **Copper (Cu)**, **Mercury (Hg)**, **Silver (Ag)**, and **Gold (Au)**, do not react with **dilute HCl** at all, and thus, no bubbles are formed.
 
• **Factors affecting rate:** Besides the nature of the metal, the rate of reaction is also influenced by the **surface area** of the metal, the **concentration** of the acid, and the **temperature** of the solution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Magnesium** has an **atomic number of 12** and belongs to **Group 2** (Alkaline Earth Metals) of the periodic table. Its high tendency to lose its **two valence electrons** makes it very reactive.
 
• In a laboratory setting, the **temperature rise** (enthalpy change) recorded during the reaction is highest for **Magnesium**, further proving it has the highest rate of reaction among the four.
 
• **Iron** reacts to form **Ferrous Chloride (FeCl2)** and **Hydrogen**, but the reaction is slow enough that it is often used in controlled school experiments to demonstrate steady gas evolution.
</ul

questions.question: Why are micro-nutrients important for plants?

options.text: They increase the size of the plant roots.
They help in the absorption of sunlight.
They are only needed for decorative plants.
They support essential functions even in small amounts.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They support essential functions even in small amounts**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Micronutrients**, often referred to as **trace elements**, are essential dietary elements required by plants in very small quantities, typically less than **10 mmole per kg** of **dry matter**.
 
• These nutrients are vital because they act as **cofactors** for **enzymes** and participate in essential **redox reactions** and **metabolic processes** within the plant cells.
 
• Statement 1 suggests they primarily increase the size of plant roots. While certain nutrients influence root architecture, this is not the defining characteristic of micronutrients as a group. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• Statement 2 claims they help in the absorption of sunlight. Sunlight absorption is the primary role of **Chlorophyll**, which contains **Magnesium** (a macronutrient); micronutrients like **Iron** only assist in its synthesis. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• Statement 3 posits they are only for decorative plants. In reality, all plants, including **agricultural crops**, **forest trees**, and **aquatic plants**, require them for survival. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• Statement 4 states they support essential functions even in small amounts. This is the fundamental definition of micronutrients, as their absence leads to **deficiency symptoms** and prevents the plant from completing its **life cycle**. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.***
 
• The **eight** essential micronutrients include **Iron (Fe)**, **Manganese (Mn)**, **Copper (Cu)**, **Molybdenum (Mo)**, **Zinc (Zn)**, **Boron (B)**, **Chlorine (Cl)**, and **Nickel (Ni)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Classification of Nutrients:**
 
 
• **Macronutrients:** These are required in large amounts (exceeding **10 mmole per kg** of dry matter). Examples include **Nitrogen (N)**, **Phosphorus (P)**, **Potassium (K)**, **Calcium (Ca)**, **Magnesium (Mg)**, and **Sulphur (S)**.
 
• **Micronutrients:** Required in minute quantities, often measured in **parts per million (ppm)** or **micrograms**.
 
 
 
• **Specific Functions of Micronutrients:**
 
 
• **Zinc (Zn):** Essential for the synthesis of **Auxin** (a plant hormone) and activates various **carboxylases**.
 
• **Boron (B):** Necessary for **pollen germination**, **cell elongation**, and **translocation of carbohydrates**.
 
• **Molybdenum (Mo):** A component of **Nitrogenase** and **Nitrate reductase**, enzymes involved in **nitrogen metabolism**.
 
• **Iron (Fe):** Required in larger amounts than other micronutrients; it is a constituent of **Ferredoxin** and **Cytochromes**.
 
 
 
• **Criteria for Essentiality:** Proposed by **Arnon and Stout** in **1939**, stating an element is essential if the plant cannot complete its **life cycle** without it and the element is directly involved in **plant metabolism**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Toxicity vs. Deficiency:** There is a narrow range of concentration at which micronutrients are optimum. Any slight decrease causes **deficiency**, while a slight increase can cause **toxicity**.
 
• **Manganese Toxicity:** An excess of **Manganese** can induce deficiencies of **Iron**, **Magnesium**, and **Calcium** by competing for uptake or binding sites.
 
• **Beneficial Elements:** Apart from the **17 essential elements**, some plants require **Sodium (Na)**, **Silicon (Si)**, **Cobalt (Co)**, and **Selenium (Se)** for specific functional needs.
 
• **Mobility:** Elements like **Nitrogen** and **Potassium** are highly **mobile**, so deficiency symptoms appear first in **older leaves**. In contrast, **Calcium** and **Iron** are **immobile**, and symptoms appear first in **younger leaves**.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is a chemical change?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rusting of iron**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **chemical change** is a process where one or more substances are transformed into new substances with entirely different **chemical properties** and **compositions**.
 
• **Rusting of iron** occurs when **iron (Fe)** reacts with **oxygen (O2)** and **moisture (H2O)** in the atmosphere to form **hydrated iron(III) oxide**, commonly known as **rust**. This is a permanent and irreversible change that results in the formation of a new chemical substance. ***Hence, option 3 is correct.***
 
• **Dissolving salt in water** is a **physical change**. Although the salt disappears from view, it still retains its chemical identity as **Sodium Chloride (NaCl)** and can be recovered back through the process of **evaporation** or **distillation**. ***Hence, option 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Cutting of paper** into smaller pieces only alters the **physical dimensions** (size and shape) of the material. The **cellulose molecules** that make up the paper do not undergo any chemical transformation into a different substance. ***Hence, option 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Melting of ice** represents a **change of state** from **solid** to **liquid**. The chemical formula for both ice and water remains **H2O**. Such phase transitions are classic examples of physical changes because they are usually **reversible**. ***Hence, option 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Chemical Changes:**
 
 
• They involve the **breaking** and **making of chemical bonds**.
 
• Common indicators include **evolution of gas**, **change in color**, **formation of a precipitate**, or **absorption/release of energy** (heat or light).
 
• Examples include **combustion (burning)** of fuels, **ripening of fruits**, **fermentation** of grapes, and **cooking of food**.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Physical Changes:**
 
 
• These changes are mostly **reversible** and do not result in the formation of a new substance.
 
• They only affect the **physical properties** such as **volume**, **density**, **viscosity**, or **state**.
 
• Examples include **stretching of a rubber band**, **magnetization of iron**, **boiling of water**, and **breaking of glass**.
 
 
 
• **Prevention of Rusting:**
 
 
• **Galvanization**: This is the process of applying a protective **zinc coating** to **steel** or **iron** to prevent rusting.
 
• **Alloying**: Mixing iron with other metals like **Chromium** and **Nickel** to produce **stainless steel**, which is resistant to corrosion.
 
• **Painting and Greasing**: Creating a barrier between the metal surface and the **moist air** to inhibit the oxidation reaction.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The chemical equation for **rusting** can be simplified as: **4Fe + 3O2 + 6H2O → 4Fe(OH)3** (which eventually dehydrates to **Fe2O3·nH2O**).
 
• In **Physical changes**, the **mass** of the individual substance remains constant before and after the change, whereas in **Chemical changes**, while the **total mass** (Law of Conservation of Mass) is conserved, the mass of the original reactants decreases as products are formed.
 
• **Digestion** is a complex biological process that involves both **physical changes** (chewing) and **chemical changes** (breakdown of molecules by enzymes and **hydrochloric acid** in the stomach).
</ul

questions.question: The image formed on the retina of the human eye is __________.

questions.question: What will be the change in kinetic energy of the particles of solid if temperature is increased?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kinetic energy increases**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **Kinetic Molecular Theory** of matter, the **temperature** of a substance is a direct measure of the average **kinetic energy** of its constituent particles.
 
• In a **solid** state, particles are held together by strong **intermolecular forces** and are arranged in a fixed, regular pattern. These particles do not move from one position to another but **vibrate** around their **fixed mean positions**.
 
• When the **temperature** of a solid is **increased**, heat energy is transferred to the particles. This energy is absorbed as **thermal energy**, which increases the **velocity** of the particles' vibrations.
 
• Since **kinetic energy** is mathematically defined as **1/2 mv²** (where **m** is **mass** and **v** is **velocity**), an increase in the speed of vibration directly results in an **increase in kinetic energy**. ***Hence, the statement that kinetic energy increases is correct.***
 
• If the **temperature** continues to rise, the **kinetic energy** eventually becomes high enough to overcome the **attractive forces** holding the particles together, leading to **melting** or a **phase transition** from **solid** to **liquid**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Solids**: 
 
 
• **Solids** have a **definite shape** and **definite volume** due to the negligible space between particles and strong **cohesive forces**.
 
• The particles in a **solid** have the **lowest kinetic energy** compared to the same substance in **liquid** or **gaseous** states at the same temperature.
 
 
 
• **Absolute Zero**:
 
 
• **Absolute Zero** is the theoretical temperature at which all **molecular motion** stops, meaning the **kinetic energy** of the particles becomes **zero**. 
 
• This temperature is defined as **0 Kelvin** or **-273.15 degrees Celsius**.
 
 
 
• **Relationship between Temperature and KE**:
 
 
• The **Average Kinetic Energy** of a particle is **directly proportional** to the **absolute temperature** (measured in **Kelvin**).
 
• This relationship is a fundamental concept in **thermodynamics** and explains why substances expand (**Thermal Expansion**) when heated, as the more energetic vibrations require more space.
 
 
 
• **Intermolecular Forces**:
 
 
• As **kinetic energy** increases with temperature, the influence of **intermolecular forces** (like **Van der Waals forces** or **Hydrogen bonding**) effectively decreases relative to the motion, eventually leading to the loss of **rigidity** in the substance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Boltzmann Constant**: The link between the **average kinetic energy** of particles and **temperature** is provided by the **Boltzmann constant** (approximately **1.38 x 10⁻²³ Joules per Kelvin**).
 
• **Internal Energy**: The **total internal energy** of a solid system includes both the **kinetic energy** of the vibrating particles and the **potential energy** associated with the chemical bonds and **intermolecular attractions**.
 
• **Specific Heat Capacity**: This is the amount of **heat energy** required to raise the **temperature** of **1 kilogram** of a substance by **1 degree Celsius** (or **1 Kelvin**), which varies depending on the **molecular structure** of the solid.
 
• **Vibrational Modes**: In complex solids, **kinetic energy** isn't just about simple back-and-forth motion; it can involve various **vibrational modes** and **rotational components** depending on the **lattice structure**.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a combination reaction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Combination Reaction** is a type of **chemical reaction** where two or more **reactants** (elements or compounds) combine to form a **single product**. The general symbolic representation is **A + B → AB**.
 
• In the reaction **C + O2 → CO2**, **Carbon** reacts with **Oxygen** to form a single product, **Carbon Dioxide**. This is a classic example of a combination reaction occurring during the **combustion** of **coal**. ***Hence, this is a combination reaction.***
 
• The reaction **2Mg + O2 → 2MgO** involves **Magnesium** ribbon burning in the presence of **Oxygen** to produce a single product, **Magnesium Oxide**, which is a white powder. ***Hence, this is a combination reaction.***
 
• In **N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3**, **Nitrogen gas** and **Hydrogen gas** combine under specific conditions of **temperature** and **pressure** to form **Ammonia**. This is industrially known as the **Haber-Bosch process**. ***Hence, this is a combination reaction.***
 
• The reaction **HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O** involves **Hydrochloric Acid** reacting with **Sodium Hydroxide** (a base) to produce **Sodium Chloride** (salt) and **Water**. Since there are **two distinct products** formed rather than one, it does not fit the definition of a combination reaction. ***Hence, this is NOT a combination reaction.***
 
• ***Therefore, the correct answer is HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Neutralization Reaction**:
 
 
• The reaction between an **Acid** and a **Base** is specifically called a **Neutralization Reaction**.
 
• In the given example, **HCl** provides **H+ ions** and **NaOH** provides **OH- ions**, which combine to form **Liquid Water**.
 
• The remaining **Sodium (Na+)** and **Chloride (Cl-)** ions form **Sodium Chloride**, a common **neutral salt**.
 
 
 
• **Double Displacement Reaction**:
 
 
• The reaction **HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O** is also categorized as a **Double Displacement Reaction**.
 
• In this process, the **cations** and **anions** of two different **compounds** switch places to form two entirely new compounds.
 
• The general formula for this type of reaction is **AB + CD → AD + CB**.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Combination Reactions**:
 
 
• These reactions are often **Exothermic** in nature, meaning they release a significant amount of **heat energy** to the surroundings.
 
• An example is the reaction of **Calcium Oxide** (Quick Lime) with **Water** to form **Calcium Hydroxide** (Slaked Lime), which releases intense heat.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Decomposition Reaction**: This is the exact **opposite** of a combination reaction. In this case, a **single reactant** breaks down into two or more **simpler products**. For instance, the **electrolysis of water** (2H2O → 2H2 + O2) is a decomposition reaction.
 
• **Displacement Reaction**: This occurs when a **more reactive element** displaces a **less reactive element** from its **aqueous salt solution**. For example, **Iron (Fe)** reacting with **Copper Sulfate (CuSO4)** to form **Iron Sulfate (FeSO4)** and **Copper (Cu)**.
 
• **Redox Reactions**: Many combination reactions, such as the burning of **Magnesium** or **Coal**, are also **Oxidation-Reduction (Redox)** reactions because they involve the **transfer of electrons** between species.
 
• **Stoichiometry**: In the provided options, the **coefficients** (like the **2** in 2Mg or the **3** in 3H2) are used to **balance** the equation, ensuring the **Law of Conservation of Mass** is followed, meaning the **number of atoms** of each element remains constant before and after the reaction.

questions.question: What is the role of a fuse in an electric circuit?

options.text: To break the circuit if the current exceeds a safe level, preventing damage
To not break the circuit if the current exceeds a safe level
To increase the current when needed
To cool down the wires during overheating

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To break the circuit if the current exceeds a safe level, preventing damage**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• An **electric fuse** is a crucial **safety device** used in electrical circuits to protect appliances and the building from **excessive current**.
 
• The primary **function** of a fuse is to **break the circuit** by melting when the flow of current exceeds a predefined **safe limit**. ***Hence, the statement in option 1 is correct.***
 
• It is always connected in **series** with the **live wire** of the circuit, ensuring that all current entering the appliance must first pass through the fuse.
 
• A fuse consists of a thin wire or strip made of a material with a **low melting point** and **high resistance**, such as an alloy of **tin and lead**.
 
• When the current is too high (due to **short-circuiting** or **overloading**), the temperature of the fuse wire rises rapidly according to **Joule’s heating effect**, causing it to melt and **interrupt the flow** of electricity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fuse Rating:** Every fuse is assigned a **current rating** (measured in **Amperes**), such as **5A** for light circuits and **15A** for heavy appliances like air conditioners or geysers. The rating indicates the **maximum current** the fuse can carry without melting.
 
• **Material Properties:** The fuse wire must have a **low melting point** so that it reacts quickly to heat. It also needs **high resistivity** compared to the copper wires used in house wiring to ensure sufficient heat is generated locally at the fuse.
 
• **Short Circuit vs. Overloading:** 
 
 
• **Short circuiting** occurs when the **live wire** and **neutral wire** come into direct contact, causing a massive surge in current.
 
• **Overloading** occurs when too many high-power appliances are connected to a **single socket**, drawing more current than the wires can handle.
 
 
 
• **Modern Alternatives:** In modern electrical installations, **Miniature Circuit Breakers (MCBs)** are often used instead of traditional fuses. Unlike fuses, which must be replaced once blown, **MCBs** simply trip and can be **reset manually**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Joule’s Law of Heating:** The heat produced in the fuse is governed by the formula **H = I²Rt**, where **I** is the current, **R** is the resistance, and **t** is the time. This law explains why a sudden increase in current (**I**) leads to a rapid increase in heat (**H**).
 
• **Placement:** A fuse is always placed at the **beginning** of the circuit to ensure that the entire system downstream is protected if the fuse **blows**.
 
• **Analysis of other options:**
 
 
• Option 2 is incorrect because the very purpose of a fuse is to **break** the circuit under unsafe conditions.
 
• Option 3 is incorrect because a fuse does not act as a transformer or booster; it cannot **increase** current.
 
• Option 4 is incorrect because a fuse does not provide **cooling**; it responds to heat by **sacrificing itself** (melting) to stop the current.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: A gardener wants to grow stronger plants with better fruit. Which pollination method should they encourage?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cross-pollination**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cross-pollination**, scientifically termed **Xenogamy**, is the process where **pollen grains** are transferred from the **anther** of a flower on one plant to the **stigma** of a flower on a different plant of the same **species**.
 
• This method is highly encouraged by gardeners and farmers because it promotes **genetic diversity** by combining the **genetic material** of two different parent plants. ***Hence, the correct answer is Cross-pollination.***
 
• The offspring produced through **cross-pollination** often demonstrate **Hybrid Vigor** (also known as **Heterosis**), which results in plants that are **stronger**, more **resilient to diseases**, and capable of producing **superior quality fruit** and **larger seeds**.
 
• Unlike **self-pollination**, which can lead to the expression of harmful **recessive traits** over generations, cross-pollination introduces new **alleles** into the population, enhancing the **evolutionary fitness** of the plants.
 
• It is an essential mechanism for **adaptation** to changing **environmental conditions**, as the varied **genotypes** produced have a better chance of surviving **pests**, **drought**, or **temperature fluctuations**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Self-pollination**:
 
 
• This occurs when **pollen** is transferred from the **anther** to the **stigma** of the same flower (**Autogamy**) or another flower on the same plant.
 
• While it ensures **seed production** when **pollinators** are scarce, it leads to **inbreeding depression**, which reduces the **vigor** and **fertility** of the lineage over time.
 
 
 
• **Geitonogamy**:
 
 
• This is a specific type of pollination where pollen from one flower is transferred to the **stigma** of another flower on the **same plant**.
 
• Functionally, it resembles **cross-pollination** because it often requires a **pollinating agent**, but genetically it is equivalent to **self-pollination** because all flowers on the plant share the same **DNA**.
 
 
 
• **Pollinating Agents**:
 
 
• Plants rely on **Biotic agents** such as **bees**, **butterflies**, **birds**, and **bats**, or **Abiotic agents** like **wind** (Anemophily) and **water** (Hydrophily) to facilitate the transfer of pollen.
 
• **Bees** are the most common **biotic pollinators**, responsible for a significant portion of the pollination in **food crops** worldwide.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Advantages of Cross-pollination**:
 
 
• It produces **progeny** with higher **viability** and better **germination rates**.
 
• It allows for the creation of **new varieties** of plants with desirable characteristics like **sweeter fruit**, **brighter flowers**, or **increased yield**.
 
• It helps eliminate **defective traits** from the **gene pool** through **genetic recombination**.
 
 
 
• **Disadvantages of Cross-pollination**:
 
 
• It is highly dependent on **external factors** like **pollinators** and **weather conditions**; if these fail, **fertilization** might not occur.
 
• Plants must invest more **energy** in producing **nectar**, **scent**, and **colorful petals** to attract **pollinators**.
 
 
 
• **Self-Incompatibility**: Many plants have developed **biological mechanisms** to prevent **self-pollination**, such as **Dichogamy** (different maturation times for male and female parts) to ensure that **cross-pollination** occurs.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of meristematic cells?

options.text: Dense cytoplasm and lack of vacuoles

questions.solution:
p data-end="57" data-start="0">The correct answer is __**Dense cytoplasm and lack of vacuoles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Meristematic cells** are a group of young cells that are in a continuous state of **cell division**. These tissues are found in the growing regions of plants, such as the tips of roots and shoots.
 
• A defining characteristic of these cells is the presence of **dense cytoplasm** and a **large, prominent nucleus**. This is because the cells are metabolically very active and require a high concentration of organelles and genetic material to support rapid division.
 
• **Meristematic cells** generally **lack vacuoles**. In mature plant cells, vacuoles serve as storage for food, waste, and provide turgidity. However, meristematic cells do not need to store these materials as they divide quickly, and a large vacuole might obstruct the process of **mitosis**. ***Hence, the third option is the correct characteristic.***
 
• The **cell walls** of meristematic tissues are **thin** and made primarily of **cellulose**. This thinness allows the cells to expand and divide without the restriction of rigid, thick walls.
 
• These cells are **compactly arranged** without any **intercellular spaces** between them, ensuring a solid mass of dividing tissue at growth points.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Classification of Meristematic Tissues:**
 
 
• **Apical Meristem**: Located at the **growing tips of stems and roots**. It is responsible for the **primary growth** of the plant, increasing its overall length.
 
• **Intercalary Meristem**: Found at the **base of leaves** or **internodes** (common in monocots like grasses). It helps in the elongation of the internodes and regrowth of parts removed by grazing animals.
 
• **Lateral Meristem**: Occurs on the sides of the plant body (e.g., **vascular cambium** and **cork cambium**). It is responsible for **secondary growth**, which increases the **girth** or thickness of the plant.
 
 
 
• **Differentiation into Permanent Tissues:**
 
 
• Once meristematic cells stop dividing, they undergo **differentiation** to become **permanent tissues**. These can be **Simple Permanent Tissues** (Parenchyma, Collenchyma, Sclerenchyma) or **Complex Permanent Tissues** (Xylem and Phloem).
 
• **Parenchyma** cells often have **large central vacuoles** for storage, which distinguishes them from meristematic cells.
 
• **Sclerenchyma** consists of **dead cells** with **thick walls** reinforced with **lignin**, providing mechanical strength.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Analysis of Incorrect Options:**
 
 
• **Dead cells with empty spaces**: This describes **Sclerenchyma** or mature **Xylem vessels**. Meristematic cells must be living to perform cell division. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Thin walls with lignin deposits**: Lignin is a complex polymer that provides rigidity and is typically found in **permanent tissues** like Sclerenchyma or Xylem, not in actively dividing meristems which require flexible cellulose walls. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Thick walls and large vacuoles**: This is a feature of mature, **differentiated cells** like Parenchyma. Thick walls would hinder the rapid expansion and division necessary for meristematic activity. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Metabolic State**: The **respiration rate** in meristematic cells is very high compared to permanent cells because of the energy required for **DNA replication** and cytoplasmic synthesis during the **cell cycle**.
 
• **Shape**: These cells are usually **isodiametric**, meaning they have roughly equal dimensions in all directions, often appearing spherical, oval, or polygonal.

__
 
• **Connective tissue** is the most diverse and abundant type of tissue in the **human body**, providing support, protection, and structural integration. **Blood** is classified as a **fluid connective tissue** because it consists of cells (**erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets**) suspended in a liquid extracellular matrix called **plasma**, and it serves to connect all systems of the body by transporting nutrients and waste. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• **Epithelial tissue** consists of tightly packed cells that form a continuous sheet, covering the external surfaces of the body and lining internal organs and cavities. **Blood** does not belong to this category; rather, epithelial tissue examples include the **epidermis of the skin** and the **inner lining of the mouth**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Muscular tissue** is specialized for **contraction** and movement. It is composed of long cells called **muscle fibers**. **Neurons**, however, are the functional units of the **nervous system**, not the muscular system. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Nervous tissue** is responsible for receiving stimuli and transmitting electrical impulses to various parts of the body. It consists of **neurons** and **glial cells**. **Muscles** are effector organs composed of **muscular tissue** that respond to nervous stimulation, but they are not nervous tissue themselves. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• Animal tissues are categorized into four primary types based on their structure and function: **Epithelial**, **Connective**, **Muscular**, and **Nervous**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Connective Tissue:**
 
 
• **Loose Connective Tissue:** Includes **Areolar tissue** (found under the skin) and **Adipose tissue** (stores **fat**).
 
• **Dense Connective Tissue:** Includes **Tendons** (connect **muscle to bone**) and **Ligaments** (connect **bone to bone**).
 
• **Specialized Connective Tissue:** Includes **Cartilage**, **Bone**, and **Blood**. Unlike other connective tissues, **blood** does not contain **fibers** like **collagen** or **elastin** unless it is clotting.
 
 
 
• **Components of Blood:**
 
 
• **Plasma:** A straw-colored fluid making up about **55%** of total blood volume, containing water, proteins, and electrolytes.
 
• **Red Blood Cells (RBCs):** Also known as **Erythrocytes**, containing **hemoglobin** for **oxygen transport**.
 
• **White Blood Cells (WBCs):** Also known as **Leukocytes**, which are part of the **immune system**.
 
• **Platelets:** Also known as **Thrombocytes**, which aid in **blood clotting**.
 
 
 
• **Functions of Tissues:**
 
 
• **Epithelial:** Functions include **protection**, **secretion**, **absorption**, and **filtration**.
 
• **Muscular:** Categorized into **Skeletal** (voluntary), **Smooth** (involuntary, found in **visceral organs**), and **Cardiac** (found in the **heart**).
 
• **Nervous:** Specialized for **excitability** and **conductivity**, allowing the body to respond to internal and external environmental changes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Origin:** Most connective tissues, including **blood** and **bone**, originate from the **mesoderm** (the middle germ layer of the embryo).
 
• **Physical Properties of Blood:** The average adult human has about **5 to 6 liters** of blood. The **pH** of human blood is slightly **alkaline**, typically ranging from **7.35 to 7.45**.
 
• **Nervous System Unit:** The **Neuron** is the longest cell in the human body, specifically designed to transmit signals over long distances, such as from the **spinal cord** to the **toes**.
 
• **Bone vs. Cartilage:** While both are specialized connective tissues, **bone** has a hard, **calcified matrix**, whereas **cartilage** has a firm but **flexible matrix** composed of **chondroitin salts**.

questions.question: Galvanisation is a method of protecting steel and iron from rusting by coating them with a thin layer of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**zinc**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Galvanisation** is a specific metallurgical process used to protect **steel** and **iron** from **rusting** by applying a thin protective coating of **zinc**.
 
• The process works on the principle of **sacrificial protection**; because **zinc** is more chemically active than **iron**, it oxidizes in preference to the **iron** or **steel** it covers. ***Hence, the option zinc is correct.***
 
• Even if the **zinc** coating is scratched or damaged, the remaining **zinc** continues to act as a **sacrificial anode**, protecting the exposed **iron** from corrosion.
 
• The most common method is **hot-dip galvanizing**, where the metal parts are submerged in a bath of molten **zinc** at a temperature of approximately **450°C** (**842°F**).
 
• Other metals like **aluminium**, **copper**, and **magnesium** are not used in the process officially defined as "galvanisation." While **aluminium** provides corrosion resistance, it is used in processes like **anodizing** or as an alloy coating. ***Hence, statements involving aluminium, copper, and magnesium are incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rusting of Iron:** 
 
 
• **Rust** is a reddish-brown flaky substance formed when **iron** reacts with **oxygen** and **moisture** (water) in the environment.
 
• The chemical formula for **rust** is typically represented as **hydrated iron(III) oxide** (**Fe2O3·nH2O**).
 
• Both **air** and **water** are essential conditions for **rusting** to occur.
 
 
 
• **Other Corrosion Prevention Methods:**
 
 
• **Painting:** Creating a barrier between the metal and the atmosphere.
 
• **Oiling and Greasing:** Used frequently for moving machine parts to repel **moisture**.
 
• **Alloying:** Mixing **iron** with metals like **chromium** and **nickel** to create **stainless steel**, which does not rust.
 
• **Electroplating:** Using **electricity** to coat a metal with a thin layer of another metal like **tin** or **chromium**.
 
 
 
• **Properties of Zinc Coating:**
 
 
• When exposed to the atmosphere, **zinc** reacts with **oxygen** to form **zinc oxide**, which further reacts with **carbon dioxide** to form **zinc carbonate** (**ZnCO3**).
 
• This **zinc carbonate** layer is a strong, insoluble material that stops further corrosion of both the **zinc** and the underlying **iron**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **History:** The term is named after the **Italian** scientist **Luigi Galvani**, though the practical application of **hot-dip galvanizing** was patented later by **Stanislas Sorel** in **1837**.
 
• **Types of Galvanization:**
 
 
• **Hot-dip Galvanizing:** Submerging the metal in molten **zinc**.
 
• **Electro-galvanizing:** A layer of **zinc** is applied using an **electric current** in an electrolyte solution.
 
• **Sherardizing:** Also known as **vapor galvanizing**, it involves heating the **iron** component in a closed drum with **zinc dust**.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Use:** This method is widely used in the **construction** of bridges, **automotive** body parts, **telecommunication** towers, and household items like **buckets** and **roofing sheets**.
 
• **Economic Impact:** By extending the life of **infrastructure**, **galvanisation** saves billions of dollars annually in **maintenance** and **replacement** costs.

questions.question: The gravitational constant (G) was first measured by ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cavendish**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Henry Cavendish**, a **British scientist**, was the first person to successfully measure the **Universal Gravitational Constant (G)** in the laboratory. This landmark achievement took place between **1797 and 1798**.
 
• The experiment is famously known as the **Cavendish Experiment**. It involved the use of a **torsion balance** to measure the extremely weak gravitational attraction between two pairs of lead spheres.
 
• While **Sir Isaac Newton** had formulated the **Law of Universal Gravitation** in his work **Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica** in **1687**, he did not calculate the value of **G**. He only established the relationship that force is proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
 
• The primary objective of Cavendish's experiment was actually to **"weigh the Earth"** by determining its **average density**. By finding the value of **G**, he was able to calculate the **Earth's mass** for the first time.
 
• The value **Cavendish** derived for the density of the Earth was **5.448 times** that of water, which is remarkably close to the modern accepted value of **5.515 g/cm³**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Isaac Newton:**
 
 
• **Newton** is credited with discovering the **Universal Law of Gravitation**, which states that every particle attracts every other particle in the universe with a force (F).
 
• The formula is **F = G(m1m2)/r²**, where **m1** and **m2** are masses and **r** is the distance between them. However, **Newton** did not have the experimental tools to measure the constant **G** himself.
 
 
 
• **Galileo Galilei:**
 
 
• **Galileo** was an **Italian astronomer and physicist** known as the "father of modern science."
 
• He performed experiments on **motion and free fall**, famously demonstrating that all objects, regardless of their mass, fall with the same **acceleration (g)** in the absence of air resistance. He did not measure the universal constant **G**.
 
 
 
• **Johannes Kepler:**
 
 
• **Kepler** was a **German astronomer** who formulated the **three laws of planetary motion** in the early **17th century**.
 
• His laws described the **elliptical orbits** of planets and the relationship between a planet's distance from the Sun and its orbital period, providing the empirical foundation for **Newton's** later work on gravity.
 
 
 
• **The Gravitational Constant (G):**
 
 
• The modern value of **G** is approximately **6.674 x 10^-11 N·m²/kg²**.
 
• It is a **scalar quantity** and is considered a **fundamental physical constant** in the universe, meaning its value is the same everywhere and at all times.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Difference between G and g:**
 
 
• **G** is the **Universal Gravitational Constant** and remains constant throughout the universe.
 
• **g** is the **acceleration due to gravity**, which is approximately **9.8 m/s²** on the surface of the **Earth** but changes depending on the **altitude, latitude**, and the planet or celestial body one is standing on.
 
 
 
• **The Torsion Balance:**
 
 
• The **torsion balance** used by **Cavendish** was originally designed by the geologist **John Michell**, who died before he could complete the experiment. **Cavendish** rebuilt the apparatus and made it much more sensitive to eliminate errors caused by **air currents and temperature changes**.

questions.question: Kamali spends a lot of time studying for examinations, including reading books and organising thoughts. Why would a scientist argue that this 'hard work' involves very little 'work' in the scientific sense?

options.text: Because displacement is necessary, and studying involves zero or minimal physical displacement of the body.
Because the activity is considered useful physical labour.
Because mental effort does not involve force.
Because energy is conserved, so work done must be zero.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Because displacement is necessary, and studying involves zero or minimal physical displacement of the body.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **Physics**, the term **work** has a very specific definition that differs from its common usage in daily life. For work to be done, a **force** must be applied to an object, and that object must undergo **displacement** in the direction of the force.
 
• The scientific formula for work is **Work (W) = Force (F) × Displacement (s) × cos(θ)**, where **θ** is the angle between the force and the direction of motion.
 
• When Kamali is studying, she may be engaging in intense **mental effort**, but if she is sitting in one place, her **displacement** relative to the earth is **zero**. Without displacement, the product in the work formula becomes **zero**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• While studying is a **useful activity** or "labour" in a socio-economic context, **Classical Mechanics** does not categorize mental concentration or internal biological processes as mechanical work. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• Mental effort does involve **internal forces** (like electrical impulses in neurons or muscle tension), but work in the scientific sense requires an **external force** causing **external displacement**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The **Law of Conservation of Energy** states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed. During studying, chemical energy from food is transformed into **heat** and **electrical signals**, but this does not mean "work done" must be zero; rather, work is a **mode of energy transfer** that is simply not occurring mechanically here. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Displacement:** It is a **vector quantity** that refers to the "how far out of place an object is"; it is the object's overall change in position from the **initial point** to the **final point**.
 
• **The Joule (J):** The **SI unit** of work and energy is the **Joule**. One Joule is defined as the amount of work done when a force of **1 Newton** displaces an object by **1 meter** in the direction of the force.
 
• **Scalar Quantity:** Even though force and displacement are **vectors**, work is a **scalar quantity**, meaning it only has **magnitude** and no direction.
 
• **Positive, Negative, and Zero Work:** 
 
 
• **Positive Work:** When force and displacement are in the **same direction** (e.g., kicking a ball).
 
• **Negative Work:** When force and displacement are in **opposite directions** (e.g., **friction** acting on a moving car).
 
• **Zero Work:** When displacement is zero, or when the force is **perpendicular (90 degrees)** to the displacement.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Case of the Stationary Wall:** If a person pushes against a **rigid wall** with all their might and becomes exhausted, the scientific work done is still **zero** because the wall does not move (**displacement = 0**).
 
• **Force and Angle:** A **coolie** carrying a heavy load on his head and walking on a **horizontal platform** does **zero work** against **gravity**. This is because the force of gravity is **downward** while the displacement is **horizontal**, creating a **90-degree angle** (cos 90° = 0).
 
• **Biological vs. Mechanical Work:** The human body consumes **ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate)** and generates **metabolic energy** even when standing still or thinking. While this is "biological work," it does not result in "mechanical work" unless an object is moved through a distance.

questions.question: A special tissue through which the foetus receives nutrition is called which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Placenta**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Placenta** is a specialized, temporary **biological organ** that develops in the **uterus** during **pregnancy** to provide a vital link between the mother and the developing **foetus**.
 
• Its primary function is to provide **nutrition** and **oxygen** to the growing foetus while simultaneously removing **carbon dioxide** and other **metabolic waste** products from the foetal blood.
 
• Structurally, the placenta is a **disc-shaped** tissue that is deeply embedded in the **uterine wall**. It contains **villi** on the foetal side of the tissue, which increases the **surface area** available for the exchange of nutrients and oxygen.
 
• On the mother's side, there are **blood spaces** that surround the villi, allowing for the efficient **diffusion** of substances like **glucose**, **amino acids**, and **vitamins** from the mother’s blood to the embryo.
 
• The placenta also acts as an **endocrine gland**, secreting essential hormones such as **hCG (human Chorionic Gonadotropin)**, **progesterone**, and **estrogen**, which are necessary to maintain the pregnancy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Uterus (Womb):**
 
 
• The **Uterus** is a hollow, muscular, pear-shaped organ located in the female pelvis. It is the site where the **fertilized egg** (embryo) implants and develops throughout the **gestation period**.
 
• In humans, the typical duration of pregnancy within the uterus is approximately **9 months** or **40 weeks**.
 
 
 
• **Fallopian Tube (Oviduct):**
 
 
• The **Fallopian tubes** are a pair of tubes through which the **egg** (ovum) travels from the **ovary** to the uterus.
 
• Crucially, the Fallopian tube is the site where **fertilization** (the union of sperm and egg) usually takes place.
 
 
 
• **Cervix:**
 
 
• The **Cervix** is the lower, narrow portion of the uterus that opens into the **vagina**.
 
• During **childbirth**, the cervix must **dilate** (widen) significantly to allow the foetus to pass through the **birth canal**.
 
 
 
• **Umbilical Cord:**
 
 
• The **Umbilical Cord** is the conduit that connects the developing embryo or foetus to the **placenta**.
 
• It contains **two arteries** and **one vein**, serving as the physical pipeline for blood exchange between the placenta and the baby's **circulatory system**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Gestation Period:** The time from **conception** to **birth** is known as the gestation period. In humans, this is roughly **280 days**.
 
• **Selective Barrier:** While the placenta allows the passage of nutrients, it also acts as a **protective barrier** against many **pathogens**, though some viruses and drugs (teratogens) can still cross it.
 
• **Passive Immunity:** The placenta allows the transfer of **antibodies** (specifically **IgG**) from the mother to the foetus, providing **passive immunity** to the newborn for the first few months of life.

questions.question: Which of the following DOES NOT use the concept of multiple reflection of sound waves?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vibrating tunning fork**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Multiple reflection of sound** is a phenomenon where sound waves bounce off several surfaces before reaching the listener, often used to amplify or direct sound in a specific path.
 
• **Megaphones** (or speaking tubes) are designed to send sound in a particular direction without spreading it in all directions. The sound waves are successfully reflected multiple times by the **conical** walls of the megaphone towards the audience. *Hence, this uses the concept of multiple reflection of sound.*
 
• A **Trumpet**, like other brass instruments, utilizes a flared shape that facilitates the **multiple reflection** of sound waves, directing the sound forward and increasing its intensity. *Hence, this uses the concept of multiple reflection of sound.*
 
• A **Stethoscope** is a medical instrument used by doctors to listen to sounds produced within the body, primarily the heart or lungs. The sound of the heartbeat reaches the doctor's ears through **multiple reflections** inside the **rubber tube** of the stethoscope. *Hence, this uses the concept of multiple reflection of sound.*
 
• A **Vibrating tunning fork** consists of two prongs that produce sound through **mechanical vibration**. It is a **source** of sound where the motion of the prongs creates compressions and rarefactions in the air. It does not rely on the internal reflection of waves to function or direct sound. *Hence, the vibrating tunning fork does NOT use the concept of multiple reflection of sound.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nature of Sound Waves:**

 
 
• Sound is a **longitudinal mechanical wave** that requires a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through a **vacuum**.
 
• The speed of sound is highest in **solids** (approximately **5960 m/s** in steel) and lowest in **gases** (about **343 m/s** in air at 20 degrees Celsius).
 
 
 
• **Laws of Reflection:**
 
 
• Sound waves follow the same **laws of reflection** as light: the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and the incident wave, reflected wave, and normal all lie in the **same plane**.
 
• Hard surfaces like **concrete walls** or **metal sheets** are good reflectors of sound, while soft surfaces like **curtains** or **carpets** are good absorbers.
 
 
 
• **Echo and Reverberation:**
 
 
• An **Echo** is the repetition of sound due to reflection. To hear a distinct echo, the minimum distance between the source and the obstacle must be roughly **17.2 meters**.
 
• **Reverberation** is the persistence of sound in an enclosed space due to repeated reflections. In **auditoriums** or **cinema halls**, roof and walls are covered with sound-absorbent materials to reduce excessive reverberation.
 
 
 
• **Tuning Fork Characteristics:**
 
 
• The **tunning fork** was invented in **1711** by British musician **John Shore**.
 
• It is typically made of **steel** or **magnesium** and is designed to emit a **pure tone** at a specific **frequency** (e.g., **440 Hz** for concert A).
 
• It is widely used in **music** for tuning instruments and in **physics laboratories** to demonstrate the properties of sound waves and **resonance**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging):** This technology uses the **reflection** of **ultrasonic waves** to measure the depth of the sea or to locate underwater objects like submarines or shipwrecks.
 
• **Ceilings of Concert Halls:** These are often **curved** so that sound, after reflection, reaches all corners of the hall uniformly, demonstrating a practical application of sound reflection in **architectural acoustics**.
 
• **Ultrasound Imaging:** In the medical field, **ultrasonic waves** are reflected off internal organs to create images (sonography), helping in the diagnosis of various health conditions.
